young.html: For parents: "The Prussian Officer" is a story of cruelty and violence, written for adults. Young readers can learn here about D. H. Lawrence and how he painted landscapes in words, and leave the story itself for later.

D. H. Lawrence was the son of a coal miner in England. He became a famous writer who loved the natural world: flowers, animals, sunlight and mountains. He could make you feel the heat of a summer road or the cool of a forest just with words.

Paint with words. Lawrence opens his story with soldiers marching on a hot day: a white road, patches of shade, green fields, and far-off mountains with snow on top. Go outside (or look out a window) and write three sentences about what you see, hear and feel. Use colors, temperatures and sounds. Read them aloud: can your family picture the place?

full.html: David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) grew up in Eastwood, a mining town in Nottinghamshire, England, and became a teacher before his novel Sons and Lovers (1913) made his name. In 1912 he traveled to Germany with Frieda von Richthofen, whom he later married, and he watched German soldiers on maneuvers in Bavaria. "The Prussian Officer" gave its name to his first collection of stories, published in London in December 1914, months after the First World War began. (Lawrence had called the story "Honour and Arms"; his editor, Edward Garnett, changed the title.)
The story opens in heat and light:

full.text: They had marched more than thirty kilometres since dawn, along the white, hot road where occasional thickets of trees threw a moment of shade, then out into the glare again. On either hand, the valley, wide and shallow, glittered with heat; dark green patches of rye, pale young corn, fallow and meadow and black pine woods spread in a dull, hot diagram under a glistening sky.
full.author: D. H. Lawrence
full.ed: The Prussian Officer and Other Stories (Duckworth & Co., London)

full.html: A proud, cold aristocratic captain becomes fixed on his young orderly, a simple, healthy peasant soldier. The captain resents the young man's easy freedom and begins to torment him with small cruelties and then outright abuse. The orderly, bewildered, feels his own inner life crushed. On the march, as the heat bears down, the tension breaks in a sudden act of violence in a forest clearing. The orderly wanders off alone, feverish and lost, toward the mountains that had stood ahead of the soldiers all through the march, as Lawrence first showed them:

full.text: But right in front the mountains ranged across, pale blue and very still, snow gleaming gently out of the deep atmosphere.
full.author: D. H. Lawrence
full.ed: The Prussian Officer and Other Stories (Duckworth & Co., London)

full.html: The story ends with both men dead. Lawrence leaves the reader with the image of the far, cool mountains the orderly never reached.

full.html: Lawrence shows what happens when one person tries to master another completely. Rank and pride let the captain bully; denied feeling turns to cruelty; and the victim's crushed life breaks out in violence that destroys them both.

Written just before the Great War, the story was read as a picture of the rigid military world of Prussia. Lawrence's real subject is the inner life of the two men: buried passion, pride, and the body's revolt.
Skimming the landscapes. Lawrence's heat, glare and distant snow carry the story's feeling: the pressure building on the road, and the longing for coolness and freedom in the mountains.

items: Hegel, earlier on this ladder, wrote of the struggle between master and servant, in which the master's power turns out to depend on the servant.
Melville's Billy Budd (published 1924) is another story of a cruel officer and an innocent young sailor.
Tolstoy and later war writers, such as Hemingway in this era, also show the soldier's world from the inside.
Freud, in this era's volumes, argued that buried feelings can break out in harmful ways.
What does power over another person do to the one who holds it?
Why can't the orderly tell anyone what is happening to him?
How can a writer use weather and landscape to show feelings?
What makes an institution, like an army, prevent or allow abuse?

questions: Why do you think the captain treated the orderly so cruelly?
What could someone being bullied by a person in authority do? Who could help?
Lawrence uses heat and mountains to show feelings. Which feelings does each stand for?
Is it ever right for an officer or a boss to have complete power over someone?
How did the story's landscape make you feel?
care: A story of cruelty, abuse of power and violence ending in two deaths, for adult readers. The lesson describes it at a general level.
